storyline: The Week That Runs on Invitation
thesis: Seville in April moves its social life into a temporary city most people cannot enter.
scene: It's twenty past one in the morning and the caseta is at the point where the chairs have been pushed back. It belongs to an accountants' association, which is not obvious from inside it. A woman who has been at work since eight is dancing sevillanas with somebody's brother-in-law and both of them know the four parts without discussing it. At the open front, two people are looking in at the party and not coming in, because they have not been asked and everyone understands the arrangement. Somebody brings out another tray. The street outside has a thousand more of these, and most of them are shut to you.

sceneAnchors.text: The fairground across the river in Los Remedios, which is an empty lot for fifty-one weeks and a gridded temporary city for one. It has named streets, working addresses and a lighting arch at the entrance. On the Monday it does not exist. By the Tuesday it has a population.

The barrio on the far bank, where a good part of the city's flamenco lives the rest of the year and where the sevillanas being danced in the casetas were learned. In April the bridges carry people across in formal dress at hours that would be strange anywhere else.

The narrow shopping street in the centre, where the dressmakers work through March on the flamenca dresses that change pattern every year and are not costume. Fittings run late. The same street in April is full of people going about an ordinary working day in a city that will be awake until four.

locals: The working day continues as normal, which is the part outsiders miss. People go to the fairground after it, arriving somewhere near midnight and leaving somewhere near four, then work again. Which caseta you are in is a question of family, employer or association, and the great majority are private. Nobody is turned away rudely; you are simply not asked. The dresses are ordered months ahead and follow the year's pattern. Horses and carriages have the ground until eight, and after that it belongs to everyone on foot.

localWord.translation: the private tent, and the invitation required to enter it
localWord.body: About a thousand of them, belonging to families, firms and associations. Most are not public. The week's social map is simply the question of whose you have been asked into.

changes: You stop assuming that access is something you can buy. The whole week runs on being known by somebody, and no amount of arriving early or paying more will substitute. It is the least transactional city you have been in, and it turns out that being outside the tent is a legitimate way to spend an evening.
start: Going out at midnight on a working night, and finding that this is when things begin rather than end. You start walking the lanes between casetas without needing to be inside one, because the music reaches the street and so does the light. Somebody eventually asks you in, which is a specific and unmistakable event. You go to work the next morning anyway.
stop: Trying to get in everywhere. The fairground is not a venue with a queue and there is no version of the week where you have seen all of it. Seville in April is arranged so that most of it is happening in rooms you are not in, and this is not a failure of the arrangement.
returns: The feeling of a city that has somewhere to be. For one week Seville has a second address and everyone knows how to get there, what to wear, and which four parts of the dance to do. None of it was explained to you and all of it is being done from memory, by people who will be at their desks by nine.
remember: The door was never locked. You simply had not been asked.

items.label: February
items.body: The city is ordinary and the fairground is an empty lot.

items.label: April
items.body: Everyone works the day and goes to a tent at midnight.

items.label: August
items.body: Forty degrees, and the same streets are abandoned by three.
